interactions.label: H2 receptor antagonists such as ranitidine are effective in treating the sneezin

params.question: H2 receptor antagonists such as ranitidine are effective in treating the sneezing and rhinorrhoea of allergic rhinitis.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: H2 receptors sit on gastric parietal cells and control acid secretion — they are not involved in allergy symptoms. Allergic rhinitis symptoms are driven by histamine acting on H1 receptors in the nose, eyes, and skin. That is why H1 antagonists, not H2 blockers like ranitidine, are used to treat allergic rhinitis.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. H2 receptors are located on gastric parietal cells and regulate acid secretion — they play no role in allergic rhinitis symptoms. Sneezing, itching, and rhinorrhoea are mediated exclusively by H1 receptors, which is why only H1 antagonists treat allergic rhinitis.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old woman with moderate-persistent allergic rhinitis and nasal congest

params.question: A 30-year-old woman with moderate-persistent allergic rhinitis and nasal congestion has been using oxymetazoline nasal spray daily for two weeks. She reports worsening congestion despite continued use. What is the most likely explanation?

answers.text: Development of IgE-mediated drug allergy to oxymetazoline

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oxymetazoline allergy is exceedingly rare. The pattern of worsening congestion after prolonged decongestant use is characteristic of rebound, not hypersensitivity.

answers.text: Rhinitis medicamentosa from prolonged topical decongestant use

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Topical decongestants like oxymetazoline cause rebound nasal congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) when used beyond 3–5 days, due to receptor downregulation and mucosal oedema.
Allergic fungal sinusitis presents with thick allergic mucin, nasal polyps, and often unilateral symptoms — not simple worsening congestion after two weeks of decongestant use.
This patient is using oxymetazoline (a sympathomimetic decongestant), not an intranasal corticosteroid. Moreover, intranasal corticosteroids do not typically cause tachyphylaxis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key clue is prolonged use of a topical decongestant beyond the recommended 3–5 day limit. This causes rebound congestion called rhinitis medicamentosa, not an allergic reaction or infection.
Well done. Rhinitis medicamentosa is a common clinical pitfall — always counsel patients to limit topical decongestant use to 3–5 days maximum.

interactions.label: Aspirin has a plasma half-life of only 15–20 minutes, yet its antiplatelet effec

params.question: Aspirin has a plasma half-life of only 15–20 minutes, yet its antiplatelet effect persists for 7–10 days. Which property best explains this discrepancy?

answers.text: Aspirin is extensively redistributed into deep tissue compartments, creating a slow-release reservoir

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aspirin is rapidly hydrolysed to salicylic acid and is not extensively tissue-sequestered. The prolonged effect is pharmacodynamic (enzyme level), not pharmacokinetic.

answers.text: Active metabolites of aspirin continue to inhibit platelet COX-1 after the parent drug is cleared

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Salicylic acid, aspirin's main metabolite, is only a weak reversible COX inhibitor and does not account for the sustained antiplatelet action.

answers.text: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1 in anucleate platelets that cannot synthesise new enzyme

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Aspirin covalently acetylates a serine residue on COX-1. Since platelets lack a nucleus, they cannot produce new enzyme, so the inhibition lasts the entire platelet lifespan of 7–10 days.

answers.text: Aspirin binds with high affinity to plasma albumin, maintaining therapeutic levels beyond its apparent half-life

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While aspirin does bind albumin, its clearance is rapid. The sustained antiplatelet effect is due to irreversible enzyme modification, not prolonged plasma levels.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is that aspirin permanently destroys COX-1 by covalent acetylation. Since platelets have no nucleus, they cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts the platelet's entire lifespan of 7–10 days.
Exactly. This irreversible mechanism is why aspirin must be stopped 7–10 days before elective surgery to allow new platelets with functional COX-1 to enter the circulation.

params.question: In an acute gouty attack, monosodium urate crystals deposited in the joint activate which intracellular sensor in synovial macrophages to trigger the inflammatory cascade?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: TLR-4 is a pattern-recognition receptor for bacterial lipopolysaccharide. While it may contribute to innate immune responses, it is not the primary intracellular sensor for urate crystal-induced inflammation.

Correct. MSU crystals are phagocytosed by synovial macrophages and activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, which cleaves pro-IL-1β into active IL-1β, driving the intense neutrophilic inflammation characteristic of acute gout.
NF-κB is a downstream transcription factor in many inflammatory pathways, not the specific intracellular sensor that detects urate crystals. The NLRP3 inflammasome is the crystal-sensing platform.
COX-2 is an enzyme producing inflammatory prostaglandins; it is a downstream effector of inflammation, not the intracellular sensor that detects urate crystals and initiates the cascade.

overallFeedback.feedback: MSU crystals specifically activate the NLRP3 inflammasome inside synovial macrophages, which cleaves pro-IL-1β into active IL-1β and recruits neutrophils — this is the central driver of acute gouty inflammation.
Well done. The NLRP3 inflammasome → IL-1β axis explains why colchicine (which disrupts inflammasome assembly) and IL-1 inhibitors are effective in acute gout.

interactions.label: Other NSAIDs such as indomethacin are used to treat acute gout, yet aspirin is s

params.question: Other NSAIDs such as indomethacin are used to treat acute gout, yet aspirin is specifically avoided. Which mechanism explains why aspirin worsens gout rather than helping it?

answers.text: Aspirin causes more gastric bleeding than other NSAIDs, increasing the risk of complications in gout

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While aspirin does carry GI risk, this is a class effect shared by all non-selective NSAIDs. It is not the specific reason aspirin is avoided in gout.

answers.text: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-2 in synovial tissue, paradoxically increasing urate crystal deposition

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1 (not selectively COX-2), and its effect on gout is renal, not synovial.

answers.text: At low doses, aspirin reduces renal urate excretion, thereby worsening hyperuricaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Low-dose aspirin competitively inhibits urate secretion in the renal tubule, raising serum uric acid levels. This drug-disease interaction is unique to aspirin among NSAIDs and can precipitate or worsen gout attacks.

answers.text: Aspirin displaces urate-lowering drugs from plasma protein binding, rendering them ineffective

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While aspirin can displace other drugs from albumin, this is not the mechanism by which it worsens gout. The issue is reduced renal urate excretion at low doses.

overallFeedback.feedback: The specific problem is that low-dose aspirin reduces uric acid excretion by the kidneys, raising serum urate levels. This worsens hyperuricaemia and can trigger gout attacks — an effect not shared by other NSAIDs like indomethacin.

Exactly. This is a key drug-disease interaction: aspirin at low doses impairs renal urate excretion, worsening the very hyperuricaemia that drives gout — making it uniquely contraindicated among NSAIDs for this condition.
